title: Intersection types (A & B) and mixing shapes
hook: An intersection type merges multiple type descriptions into one value that must satisfy all of them at once — like a user who is both an employee and a manager.

blocks.text: An **intersection type** is written `A & B` and means "this value has every member of A **and** every member of B." For object types, TypeScript **merges** properties — the result must include the full combined shape. For primitives, `string & number` collapses to **`never`** because no value can be both. Intersections are the TypeScript way to compose mixins, layer capabilities onto a base type, and express "implements multiple interfaces" without a class hierarchy — closer to C# multiple interface implementation than to C# class inheritance.

entries.plainDefinition: A type that requires a value to satisfy all constituent types simultaneously. Object intersections merge fields.
entries.example: `Person & Employee` — must have name fields and employeeId.

entries.plainDefinition: When two object types are intersected, their properties are combined. Conflicting property types are themselves intersected.
entries.example: `{ a: string } & { b: number }` → `{ a: string; b: number }`.

entries.plainDefinition: When the same property has incompatible types in both sides, the property type becomes never and the whole intersection may be unusable.

blocks.text: Framework code often layers behavior: a React component that is both `React.FC` and has static metadata, or a repository that is both readable and writable. Intersections let you **compose** types without creating a deep inheritance tree. They pair naturally with utility types like `Partial<T>` and `Readonly<T>` (covered in the readonly topic). C# achieves similar goals with `: IRead, IWrite` on a class; TypeScript does it purely at the type level on plain objects and functions.

blocks.title: Union vs intersection
blocks.body: Union (`|`) is **OR** — the value is one of the types. Intersection (`&`) is **AND** — the value must satisfy all types. `A | B` widens what you accept; `A & B` narrows what you produce.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Merge two object interfaces
items.body: `type Admin = User & { role: "admin"; permissions: string[] }` — result has all User fields plus admin fields.

items.title: Intersect function types
items.body: Function intersections become **overloaded** call signatures merged together — each call must be valid for at least one signature.

items.title: Watch for conflicts
items.body: Same property name with incompatible types → `never`. Same property with compatible subtypes → the intersection of the property types.

items.title: Combine with unions
items.body: `(A | B) & C` distributes: `(A & C) | (B & C)`. Order and parentheses matter for readability.

snippet.label: Merging interfaces with intersection
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–9: two interfaces describe separate concerns. Line 11: `&` merges them — `AuditedUser` requires all six properties. Lines 13–18: the object literal must satisfy the full intersection or excess/missing property errors appear.

snippet.label: Mixin-style function intersection
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–2: capability traits as object types. Line 4: intersection requires both `id` and `toJSON`. Lines 6–13: the returned object implements every member — no class keyword needed.

snippet.label: Conflicting properties become never
snippet.explanation: Line 1: both sides declare `id` but with incompatible types. Line 2: TypeScript intersects `string & number` → `never`. Lines 4–5: no value can satisfy `id: never` — the type is intentionally uninhabitable.

snippet.label: Intersection with union — distributing AND over OR
snippet.explanation: Line 5: `(Cat | Dog) & Named` means every pet has a `name` plus either cat or dog fields. Line 8: `kind` and `name` are on all branches — safe without extra narrowing. `meow` still requires narrowing to `Cat`.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Confusing `A & B` with `A | B` — intersection requires all members. Creating `string & number` accidentally and wondering why nothing assigns. Expecting intersection to deep-merge nested objects — only top-level properties merge; nested objects need mapped types (module 12).

blocks.text: Intersection of function types produces an overloaded callable — each invocation must match at least one constituent signature. With generics, `T & U` constrains `T` and `U` simultaneously — useful in `extends` clauses. **Interface merging** (declaration merging) is a separate mechanism: two `interface Foo` blocks merge like intersection but at declaration level. For API design, prefer intersection over inheritance when combining orthogonal capabilities (logging + caching + auth). Reducing `A & B` when `A extends B` simplifies to `A`.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Harder to read than one interface

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying intersection is OR. Not knowing conflicting properties become never. Claiming intersection deep-merges nested objects. Unable to contrast with C# multiple interface implementation.

interviewTakeaways: Intersection `A & B` means the value satisfies ALL constituent types — AND, not OR.
Object intersections merge properties; conflicting types on the same key become never.
Function intersections merge into overloaded call signatures.
`(A | B) & C` distributes to `(A & C) | (B & C)`.
60s: Intersection composes shapes. Union picks alternatives. C# uses multiple interfaces; TS uses & at the type level. Watch property conflicts.
commonPitfalls: Expecting nested object merge from top-level intersection only.
Strong answer: 'Intersection is AND. Properties merge. Conflicts → never. C# class : IA, IB is the nominal cousin.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Runtime mixin patterns with spread or Object.assign mirror intersection intent, but JS does not verify the combined shape at compile time.
C# comparison: `class Repo : IRead, IWrite` is nominal. TypeScript `Readable & Writable` is structural — any object with both shapes qualifies.
